findings.location: forms_records[3] ('The elements a Massachusetts controlled-substance prescription must state are ...')
findings.problem: The section states a closed list of the required elements of a Massachusetts controlled-substance prescription. The list reproduces M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 22(a) only. It omits the quantity of dosage units, which 105 CMR 721.020(D)(3) requires on every prescription generated in the Commonwealth, and it gives the veterinary prescription as the sole exception to the patient name-and-address requirement, whereas 105 CMR 721.020(D)(4) also leaves that field blank for a prescription for naloxone or another Department-approved opioid antagonist and for prescriptions issued under 105 CMR 721.070(A)(7) and (A)(12).
findings.rationale: 105 CMR 721.003 applies 105 CMR 721.000 to all Prescriptions issued by practitioners or reduced to writing by pharmacists, and 105 CMR 721.020(D)(3) requires 'name, dosage, and strength per dosage unit of the controlled substance prescribed, and the quantity of dosage units'. Massachusetts Schedule VI is a Massachusetts controlled-substance schedule (105 CMR 700.002(F)), so a Schedule VI prescription must carry the quantity. The section's own second learning objective is to 'Apply Massachusetts prescription elements', and the listed practice question MA-Q-0118 turns on which fields are mandatory, so a candidate could conclude from this section that a Schedule VI prescription with no quantity of dosage units is complete.

findings.location: practice_question_ids: MA-Q-0120, read against decision_logic[2], quick_review[5]-[6], role_duties[2] and common_traps[4]
findings.problem: MA-Q-0120 is a select-all-that-apply question whose correct set is A, B and C. Choice A ('The pharmacies should act on the patient's transfer request in a timely manner rather than impose a blanket no-transfer rule') rests on 247 CMR 9.14(1), and distractor D ('Massachusetts requires the transferring pharmacy to charge the patient a transfer fee') is refuted only by 247 CMR 9.14(3). The section teaches 247 CMR 9.14(4) alone: remaining refills, the one-year bar and the certified-technician route. It never states the duty to transfer at the patient's or agent's request in a timely manner, the pharmacy's ability to act as the patient's agent, or the prohibition on charging a transfer fee.
findings.rationale: 247 CMR 9.14(1) provides that 'A pharmacy shall transfer a prescription to another pharmacy, at the request of a patient or his or her agent, in a timely manner so as not to delay patient therapy', 9.14(2) permits the pharmacy to act as the patient's agent, and 9.14(3) provides that 'A pharmacy may not charge a fee for transferring a prescription.' A candidate working solely from this section can reach B and C but has no basis to select A and no basis to reject D, so on a select-all-that-apply item the listed practice question is not answerable from the section.

findings.location: timing_deadlines[1] ('Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription validity') and decision_logic[3]
findings.problem: The Schedule VI one-year validity clock is taught as the only date gate on a Schedule VI prescription. A Schedule VI prescription issued by an authorized out-of-state practitioner is fillable in Massachusetts only if it was issued within the preceding 30 days, under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c), which by its terms reaches schedules III to VI inclusive.
findings.rationale: Applied to out-of-state facts, the section's clock returns the wrong answer: at 40 days a Schedule VI prescription is inside the 247 CMR 9.04(12) year but outside the s. 18(c) window. The material is not lost across the seam, because SG-MA-OUTSTATE-PRESCRIPTIONS carries the 30-day limit and MA-Q-0424 is mapped there, so this is a cross-reference gap rather than a contradiction; the criterion is not failed on that basis.

findings.location: decision_logic[3] condition ('presented more than one year after its issue date, or with no refills remaining and the prescriber cannot be reached in time')
findings.problem: The condition can be read as attaching the inability to obtain prescriber authorization only to the second branch, so an expired Schedule VI prescription would appear to permit the 14-day continuation without first attempting the prescriber.
findings.rationale: 247 CMR 9.04(12) conditions the professional-judgment continuation on the pharmacist being 'unable to obtain prescriber authorization in a timely manner' in both the expiry case and the no-remaining-refills case. The section's exceptions[1] entry states the condition correctly for both branches, so the section is internally recoverable and the criterion is not failed.

authorities_checked.exact_section: 105 CMR 700.002(F) (Schedule VI: all prescription drugs not included in any other schedule)
105 CMR 700.001 definition of Additional Drug; 105 CMR 700.012(A)(1)-(A)(6); 105 CMR 700.012(C)(8)
247 CMR 8.04(4)(d) (certified pharmacy technician may perform Schedule VI transfers only, with pharmacist-on-duty approval)
M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(a), (b), (c) including the closing sentence excluding Schedule VI
M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c) (out-of-state Schedule III through VI, 30-day filling window)
21 CFR 1306.25(a) (one-time refill transfer for federal Schedules III-V)

results.summary: Legally accurate on every substantive proposition I could check against primary text. 105 CMR 700.002(F), 247 CMR 9.04(10), (12), (14) and (15), 247 CMR 9.14(4)(a)-(c), 247 CMR 8.04(4)(d), 105 CMR 721.070(A)(9), 105 CMR 721.020(F)-(G), 105 CMR 721.040(A) and (C), 105 CMR 700.012(A)(5) and (C)(8) and M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(a)-(c) all read as the section states them, including the hard distinction between the 247 CMR 9.14(4)(c) transfer year and the 247 CMR 9.04(12) validity year, the 247 CMR 9.04(15) institutional sterile compounding exclusion, and the correct observation that the 21 CFR 1306.25(a) one-time refill transfer limit cannot reach a schedule that exists only in Massachusetts. Two defects stop a KEEP. The required-elements list is presented as complete but reproduces only M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 22(a) and drops the quantity of dosage units that 105 CMR 721.020(D)(3) requires. And the mapped practice question MA-Q-0120 cannot be answered from the section: two of its five choices turn on 247 CMR 9.14(1) and 9.14(3), neither of which the section teaches. Both are additive repairs.

findings.location: forms_records[3] and decision_logic[5] (emergency follow-up prescription face marking)
findings.problem: The section teaches that the emergency follow-up prescription 'bears Authorization for Emergency Dispensing on its face'. The federal rule the section itself identifies as controlling this event requires the face to carry both that phrase and the date of the oral order, and requires the pharmacist to annotate an electronic follow-up record with the original authorization and the date of the oral order.
findings.rationale: 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4) provides that the follow-up prescription 'shall have written on its face “Authorization for Emergency Dispensing,” and the date of the oral order', and adds 'For electronic prescriptions, the pharmacist must annotate the record of the electronic prescription with the original authorization and date of the oral order.' 105 CMR 721.060(B)(4) requires the same document to 'comply with federal and state law', so the federal face content governs in Massachusetts. The section carries a forms_records entry dedicated to this document and states only half of what must appear on it.

findings.location: decision_logic[5] ('expect the follow-up within seven business days') and quick_review[5]
findings.problem: The operative decision step for emergency oral Schedule II dispensing tells the pharmacist to expect the practitioner's follow-up within seven business days, with no federal qualifier. On Massachusetts facts the controlling period is the federal seven days from the oral authorization, which is shorter. A pharmacist who follows the decision step would let the controlling deadline pass and would not make the DEA notification when it is due.
findings.rationale: 105 CMR 721.060(B)(4) gives seven business days, but 105 CMR 721.060(A) requires an emergency written or oral prescription to comply with all other prescription requirements 'including requirements outlined in 105 CMR 721.070(B)', and 721.070(B) expressly yields to 'such shorter period that is required by federal law'; 721.060(B)(4) itself requires compliance with federal law. 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4) requires delivery within 7 days after the oral authorization and provides that the pharmacist's failure to notify the nearest DEA office voids the authority to have dispensed without a written prescription. The section states the correct rule three times elsewhere (ma_vs_federal[0], timing_deadlines[3], common_traps[5]), so the decision block contradicts the rest of the section at the point a candidate would actually apply it.

findings.location: quick_review[5] and exceptions[3] (emergency dispensing on 'written or orally transmitted authorization')
findings.problem: The section repeats the Massachusetts formulation that in an emergency a pharmacist may dispense a Schedule II controlled substance on the practitioner's 'written or orally transmitted authorization' with the practitioner's actual signature excused, without noting that federal law has no such written route.
findings.rationale: 21 CFR 1306.11(a) permits a pharmacist to dispense a Schedule II controlled substance only pursuant to a written prescription signed by the practitioner (or an electronic prescription), 'except as provided in paragraph (d)', and paragraph (d) reaches only oral authorization. 105 CMR 721.060(B)(2) excuses 'the actual signature of the prescribing practitioner', so the written branch of the Massachusetts emergency provision has no federal counterpart. The section elsewhere handles the MA-versus-federal seam on this same regulation carefully, so the omission is a gap rather than an error, and the criterion is not failed on it.

authorities_checked.exact_section: 105 CMR 721.010 (Failover, Emergency Situation, Oral Prescription, Prescription); 721.020(A), (F), (G)(1)-(3); 721.040(A), (C)
21 CFR 1306.21(a) (no federal follow-up prescription deadline for an oral Schedule III-V prescription)

results.summary: The hardest parts of this section are right. The Failover definitional limit is exactly 105 CMR 721.010 ('a document that originates as a schedule VI Electronic Prescription, but experiences an unforeseen defect ... and is converted to a computer generated facsimile'), the three 105 CMR 721.020(G) conditions are correctly placed downstream of that definition, the separation of a Schedule II-V transmission outage under 105 CMR 721.070(A)(2) from a Failover is correct, and the observation that only 105 CMR 721.070(A)(3) is applied for and held while the remaining exceptions are categorical matches both 721.070(A) and M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(h). The claim that the only shorter federal follow-up period is the 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4) seven days also checks out, because 21 CFR 1306.21(a) imposes no follow-up deadline on an oral Schedule III-V prescription. Two defects stop a KEEP, both on the emergency Schedule II pathway: the decision-logic step states the Massachusetts seven business days without the shorter controlling federal seven days that the rest of the section correctly identifies, and the follow-up document's required face content omits the date of the oral order that 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4) requires alongside 'Authorization for Emergency Dispensing'. All three mapped practice questions (MA-Q-0116, MA-Q-0123, MA-Q-0382) are answerable from the section and none is contradicted by it.

findings.location: learning_objectives[1], quick_review[2] and [4], decision_logic[0]-[1], role_duties[0], exceptions[1]
findings.problem: The section attaches the mandatory verification gate to out-of-state Schedule III through V prescriptions (M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c)) and to the out-of-state Schedule II NARCOTIC route (s. 18(d1/2)) only. It never states that s. 18(d), the out-of-state NONNARCOTIC Schedule II route, independently requires the filling pharmacist to determine authenticity and validity and to verify the prescription by telephone or other means, and forbids the fill where verification cannot be obtained. The decision tree sends an out-of-state nonnarcotic Schedule II prescription (amphetamine, methylphenidate and the like) straight to the five-day presentation window with no verification step, and the express contrast drawn at quick_review[4] and exceptions[1] tells the candidate that the narcotic route is where authentication and verification live.
findings.rationale: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d) provides: 'A registered pharmacist filling a prescription under the provisions of this paragraph shall determine, in accordance with professional standards and personal judgment, that such prescription is authentic and valid; and shall verify such prescription by telephone or other means. A pharmacist shall not fill a prescription for which said verification cannot be obtained.' That is the same mandatory language the section correctly reports for s. 18(c) and s. 18(d1/2). A candidate who applies this section to an out-of-state nonnarcotic Schedule II prescription would fill it inside the five-day window without the verification the statute makes a precondition of the fill. The section's declared subtopic is 'Presentation windows and the verification gate' and the section elects to teach all three out-of-state pathways, so the omission is inside its declared scope rather than outside it.

findings.problem: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c) places two distinct duties on the filling pharmacist: a general duty, for every out-of-state prescription in schedules III to VI inclusive, to determine in accordance with professional standards and personal judgment that the prescription is authentic and valid; and, layered on top for schedules III to V only, a duty to verify the prescription by telephone or other means. The section teaches only the narrower proviso. As written it leaves an out-of-state Schedule VI prescription with no stated pharmacist duty at all, and it leaves the pharmacist's general authenticity and validity determination unstated for the whole III-VI range.
findings.rationale: s. 18(c) reads: 'It is the duty of the registered pharmacist who is filling a prescription under this paragraph to determine, in accordance with professional standards and personal judgment, that such prescription is authentic and valid; provided, however, that if the substance is in schedules III to V, inclusive, the registered pharmacist shall verify the prescription by telephone or other means.' The proposition the section omits is exactly the one that the mapped practice question MA-Q-0424 uses as its distractor D ('Schedule VI prescriptions from another state require no pharmacist authenticity or validity judgment'). MA-Q-0424 remains answerable because its single best answer C is derivable from what the section does teach, so practice_question_mapping is not failed, but the section supplies no affirmative basis to reject D.

findings.location: Section as a whole, read as the candidate's decision procedure for an out-of-state prescription
findings.problem: Because the verification gate is presented as a Schedule III-V feature plus a narcotic Schedule II feature, the section as a whole distorts Massachusetts law for the third pathway it teaches. A candidate using it as intended would apply the wrong procedure to a fact pattern the section explicitly invites, namely an out-of-state nonnarcotic Schedule II prescription within five days of issue.
findings.rationale: The distortion is produced by the section's own structure rather than by any single wrong sentence: every individual statement about s. 18(c), s. 18(d1/2), s. 18(d3/4) and the Department copy is accurate, but the omission of the s. 18(d) gate in a section organised around 'the verification gate' converts a completeness gap into a misleading decision procedure.

findings.location: timing_deadlines[4] ('Remaining portion of that partially dispensed prescription') and forms_records[2]
findings.problem: The section teaches the 30-day remainder clock and the patient-record notation for a partially dispensed out-of-state Schedule II prescription, but not that only the same pharmacy that dispensed the lesser quantity may dispense the remaining portion.
findings.rationale: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) provides 'only the same pharmacy that originally dispensed the lesser quantity shall dispense the remaining portion', and 105 CMR 721.055(B)(1) states the same limit. It sits in the same sentence of the statute as the timing limits the section does teach, so a candidate asked whether a second pharmacy may complete the fill has no basis in the section. Low rather than higher because the section's declared objective for this material is the five-day / five-day distinction and the remainder clock.

authorities_checked.exact_section: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a) (written or electronic Schedule II prescription invalid 30 days after issuance)
21 CFR 1306.22(a) (federal six-month Schedule III and IV filling and refilling clock)

results.summary: Every window in this section checks out against M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18: the 30-day out-of-state filling window for schedules III to VI in s. 18(c), the five-day window in s. 18(d) and s. 18(d1/2) with their different issuing-state conditions, the s. 18(d3/4) five-day initial partial dispensing limit and 30-day remainder clock (mirrored at 105 CMR 721.055(A)-(B)), the s. 18(c) seven-day request record for an oral Schedule III-V prescription, and the anonymised Department copy within 30 days after the filling. The characterisation of the federal 21 CFR 1306.22(a) six-month clock as a refill clock that cannot license a fill Massachusetts no longer permits is also correct. The section nevertheless fails on the duty it advertises. Its declared subtopic is 'Presentation windows and the verification gate', it teaches all three out-of-state pathways, and it names the mandatory verification gate for only two of them. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d) requires the filling pharmacist to determine authenticity and validity and to verify an out-of-state NONNARCOTIC Schedule II prescription by telephone or other means, and forbids the fill where verification cannot be obtained; the section's decision tree omits that step entirely and, by naming verification for the narcotic route alone, implies its absence. It also drops the s. 18(c) general authenticity-and-validity determination that reaches the whole III-VI range including Schedule VI. Repairing this changes a learning objective, two quick-review lines, the decision spine and the role-duties block, so the disposition is MAJOR_REWRITE rather than MINOR_EDIT. All four mapped practice questions remain answerable from the section and none is contradicted by it.
